subject: Archaeology
title: Roman Aqueducts: Water for Millions
description: A short lesson to help you apply Roman Aqueducts: Water for Millions.

hook.text: Rome's aqueducts delivered 300 million gallons of water daily — more per person than many modern cities provide.

buildup.text: Eleven aqueducts fed Rome, some stretching 60 miles from mountain springs. Water flowed by gravity alone.

discovery.text: The Pont du Gard in France stands 160 feet tall and carried water across a valley for 500 years without pumps.

twist.text: Romans used lead pipes inside cities. Some historians blamed lead poisoning for the empire's decline — but levels were low.

climax.text: Some Roman aqueducts still carry water today. Engineers in the 21st century have not improved on the basic design.

punchline.text: Gravity-fed water with no pumps and no electricity. Still running.

quiz.question: How did Roman aqueducts move water over long distances?
options: Slave-powered pumps pushed water uphill through pipes
Water flowed entirely by gravity from mountain springs
Windmills at relay stations moved water through the system
